props.title: The Conspirators
props.initialSlug: Nazi resistance fighter seeks justice in Lisbon

sections.content: **The Conspirators** (1944) emerges as a fascinating entry in Warner Bros.' wave of WWII-era spy thrillers, following the massive success of Casablanca (1942). Set in neutral Portugal, it captures the same smoky intrigue and resistance fighter drama that made Casablanca a hit, though with less memorable results. Paul Henreid, who played Victor Laszlo in Casablanca, takes the lead here as a Dutch resistance fighter, with Hedy Lamarr as his mysterious love interest. The film exemplifies Hollywood's intense focus on European resistance stories during WWII, joining films like Watch on the Rhine (1943) and To Have and Have Not (1944).

sections.content: Director Jean Negulesco, who would later become known for CinemaScope spectacles like **Three Coins in the Fountain** (1954), brings a noir-influenced style to The Conspirators. The film's shadowy photography by Arthur Edeson (who also shot Casablanca) creates a constant sense of danger and uncertainty. This visual approach became a template for subsequent wartime thrillers like The Mask of Dimitrios (1944) and Ministry of Fear (1944), where European cities became labyrinths of betrayal and espionage.

The film's portrayal of wartime Lisbon as a hotbed of spies and intrigue reflects historical reality - Portugal's neutrality made it a crucial transit point for refugees and intelligence operations. This setting would be revisited in later films like **The House on 92nd Street** (1945) and **13 Rue Madeleine** (1947), establishing a sub-genre of WWII spy films focused on neutral territories rather than direct combat zones. sections.content: Like many wartime films, The Conspirators blends romance with propaganda elements, though less overtly than contemporaries like **Mrs. Miniver** (1942) or **Mission to Moscow** (1943). The love story between Henreid and Lamarr's characters serves as a metaphor for the alliance between occupied nations and their supporters, a common theme in 1940s Hollywood. The film's resistance fighter narrative helped reinforce American support for European allies while providing entertainment value through its romantic subplot.
